title: Ambiguous Strategic Classification
claim: Revealing a set of possible rules shrinks the reachable region and lets a simple model express a nonlinear effective boundary with lower burden.
layout: 3 panels left-to-right: geometric setup, behavior taxonomy, three-way comparison with burden captions
description: Three panels of 2-D geometric sketches. Panel A shows a slanted purple line (the realized classifier h) with yellow lines (possible classifiers h'1, h'2). Their intersection is a purple grid-hatched region labeled AOP, the area of positive classification. A green-hatched strip marks movement and a grey-hatched strip marks suppressed movement. A legend sits at the lower left. Panel B uses the same geometry with circle points and arrows to show strategic behaviors: moving without need, moving more than needed, too far to move, no need to move, and could have moved had h been known. Panel C compares non-strategic, strategic and ambiguous classifiers as blue negative and green positive regions around a notched boundary. Red areas mark gaming or burden, and the ambiguous panel has yellow diagonal lines. Green and red captions underneath summarize burden and errors. The eye goes first to the purple AOP in A and the red blobs in C.
caption: (A) The ambiguous strategic setup, demonstrated for discrete ambiguity with $\amb=\{h,h'_1,h'_2\}$. Points move only if they can reach the AoP (purple). Adding possible classifiers $h'$ suppresses movement (grey) by shrinking the AoP and consequently the movement region (green). Points are $x$ classified as positive (yellow) if either $h(x)=1$ or they can move. (B) Ambiguity gives rise to more nuanced strategic behavior and outcomes. (C) Simple example comparing optimal non-strategic, strategic, and ambiguous strategic classifiers. For the non-strategic classifier, movement (purple region) enables gaming behavior. For the strategic classifier, movement (purple region) induces burden, and linearity entails errors. The ambiguous strategic classifier (purple line) leverages ambiguity (yellow lines) to express a non-linear effective boundary that separates that data and entails low social burden for points that move (yellow region).
abstract: A common assumption in strategic classification is that the classifier is public knowledge. However, it remains unclear whether, and why, a system would choose to commit to full disclosure. We study a setting in which regulation requires the system to disclose some, but not all, of the information. This induces a learning task in which the learner must jointly optimize the classifier and the uncertainty surrounding it. To this end, we adopt from robust mechanism design the notion of ambiguity, which in our setting allows the learner to reveal a set or range of possible classifiers, while privately choosing which of them to ultimately realize. We investigate how ambiguity affects the learning task, develop efficient algorithms for computing best-responses and training, and empirically explore strategic learning and its outcomes in this novel setting and using our approach.
